en: Theragāthā 21.1 Mahānipāta Paṭhamavagga (First Chapter)
The Verses of the Elder Vaṅgīsa:
“Truly, while I was still dwelling at home, I have gone forth from the household life into homelessness.”
Thoughts run wild;
these are the audacious ones from the dark side.
They are like sons of high-born warriors, great archers.
Trained and wielding firm bows,
they would surround one from all sides—
a thousand who do not flee.
Even if even more women than this were to come,
they would not cause me any affliction.
Firmly established in the Dhamma—
this I have heard from the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun, as my witness.
The path leading to Nibbāna—
therein my mind delights.
While I am dwelling thus,
You approach me, O Evil One;
I shall deal with Death in such a way that you will not even see my path.
Having abandoned both aversion and attachment,
and all thoughts connected with the household life,
one should not create any mental thicket anywhere.
That bhikkhu is one who has attained nibbāna and is established in it—
whatever form exists here on earth or in the air,
whatever is included in the world or immersed in the realm of form.
All that is impermanent decays;
having realized this, the liberated ones live accordingly.
People, however, are infatuated with acquisitions.
Regarding what is seen, heard, touched, and sensed— here,
O unshaken one, dispel desire.
The sage who is not smeared by these is called "one who has crossed over."
Then those sixty [monks], possessed of applied thought,
being ordinary persons, were settled in what is not the Dhamma;
yet for one who has entered the faction, there is nothing anywhere—
But that bhikkhu was not one who grasped at what is offensive;
he was steadfast, long concentrated,
free from guile, wise, and without envy.
The sage has attained the state of peace;
having attained final nibbāna through dependent origination, he awaits the time.
Abandon conceit, Gotama.
Abandon the path of conceit entirely;
for one who is infatuated with the path of conceit will long remain full of remorse.
People smeared by deceit and struck down by pride fall into hell;
these people grieve for a long time.
Those struck down by pride are reborn in hell.
But the bhikkhu who has conquered the path and practices rightly never grieves.
He experiences fame and happiness;
they call him a "Dhamma-seer" because of that very state.
Therefore, one who is free from harshness and diligent here—
Having abandoned the hindrances, he is purified;
having abandoned conceit without remainder,
the one who has brought an end through clear knowledge is a peaceful sage.
“I am burning with sensual lust;
my mind is consumed by fire.
Please tell me, how may I find relief?”
“Out of compassion, O Gotama.
“Because of a perversion of perception,
your mind is burning with fever.”
Avoid the sign that is beautiful and associated with lust;
develop the mind through the meditation on the foul.
One-pointed and well-composed;
let mindfulness directed toward the body be yours,
and be full of disenchantment.
Cultivate the signless and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit; then,
through the full comprehension of conceit, [you shall be liberated].
"You shall live at peace.
"One should speak only those words by which one does not torment oneself;"
And that which does not harm others—
that indeed is well-spoken speech.
One should speak only words that are pleasant.
That speech which is welcomed with joy,
and which, without taking up any evil,
speaks what is pleasing to others.
Truth indeed is the deathless word;
this is the eternal Dhamma.
In truth, in the goal, and in the Dhamma—
The virtuous say they are firmly established in that speech which the Buddha speaks for the sake of attaining the security of Nibbāna.
For the making of an end to suffering—
that indeed is the supreme of words.
The wise one of profound insight,
Skilled in what is the path and what is not the path,
Sāriputta of great wisdom teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus.
He teaches in brief and speaks in detail;
his voice is like that of the sālikā bird.
Inspiration arises within him. As he teaches it,
they hear his sweet voice.
With hearts uplifted and joyful through his essence, which is delightful, worth hearing, and sweet.
“Monks, they cross over by means of the ear.
“Today, on the fifteenth day for purification,
five hundred monks have assembled.”
The sages, having severed the fetters and bonds,
are free from distress and have exhausted further becoming;
they are like a wheel-turning monarch.
Surrounded by his ministers,
he traverses this entire earth as far as the ocean’s edge.
Thus do the disciples attend upon the unsurpassed Caravan-Leader who has conquered all battles.
Possessing the threefold knowledge, having abandoned death—
these are all the sons of the Blessed One;
here, no "straw" is found.
I pay homage to the Kinsman of the Sun, the slayer of the arrow of craving,
together with more than a thousand bhikkhus.
He attends upon the Sugata as he teaches the stainless Dhamma,
Nibbāna, which is free from fear from every side.
They hear the stainless Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One;
truly, the Fully Awakened One shines forth.
Honored by the community of monks:
"The Blessed One is named Nāga,
the seventh sage among sages."
Having become like a great cloud,
you rain down upon your disciples;
having emerged from your dwelling during the day, you shower them with the Dhamma.
Out of a desire to see the Teacher,
O Great Hero, the disciple Vaṅgīsa pays homage at your feet.
“Having overcome Māra’s path and way,
he wanders having shattered the bolts;
behold him, the one who effects release from bondage.”
Having analyzed it as if dividing a portion of nectar,
he has proclaimed the manifold path for the purpose of crossing over the flood.
And in that deathless state thus proclaimed,
those who see the Dhamma stand firm and unshakable;
they are light-makers, having pierced through with deep insight.
He saw the transcendence of all standpoints;
having known and realized it,
he taught the supreme state to the tenfold assembly.
When the Dhamma has been so well-taught,
what negligence can there be for those who understand the Dhamma?
Therefore, indeed, in the teaching of that Blessed One—
“Diligent, one should always train in paying homage.
“The Elder Koṇḍañña, who awakened after the Buddha, was one of fierce exertion;”
One who frequently attains the blissful states of seclusion—
whatever is to be attained by a disciple.
By one who acts according to the Teacher’s instruction,
all that is attained through training with heedfulness.
Mahānubhāva, a possessor of the three knowledges,
skilled in discerning the minds of others,
Koṇḍañña, the heir of the Buddha.
He paid homage at the Teacher’s feet.
[The Buddha said: “To the Sage seated on the mountain slope, who has gone beyond suffering;”
The disciples, possessors of the threefold knowledge who have abandoned death, attend upon him;
he surveys them with his mind.
Moggallāna possesses great psychic power;
he thoroughly investigates their minds,
which are liberated and free from acquisitions.
Thus, the sage who has reached the further shore of suffering is endowed with all factors and perfected in manifold ways.
“They wait upon Gotama.
“Just as the moon shines in a cloudless sky,
and the sun shines free from stain;”
“Even so, O Aṅgīrasa, you, the Great Sage,
outshine the entire world with your glory.
“In former times we wandered about intoxicated by poetry;”
From village to village, from city to city,
we then saw the Perfectly Awakened One,
who has reached the further shore of all phenomena.
Thus the Sage, who has gone beyond suffering, taught the Dhamma to me;
having heard the Dhamma, we gained confidence.
Faith arose within us.
Having heard his words concerning the aggregates and the sense bases, [we understood].
Having understood the elements,
I went forth into the homeless life for the sake of many indeed.
Tathāgatas appear in the world—
those among women and men who act according to the Teaching.
Truly, it was for their sake that the Sage attained enlightenment—
for the sake of both the monks and the nuns.
Those who have seen the state free from impurity—
well-taught by the Visionary One,
the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
The four noble truths,
out of compassion for living beings:
suffering and the origin of suffering.
And the transcendence of suffering,
and the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the stilling of suffering.
Thus have these been spoken by him;
I have seen them exactly as they are.
My own true goal has been attained.
Thus was the Buddha’s teaching proclaimed:
"How welcome indeed was my arrival in the presence of the Buddha!"
Among well-classified phenomena,
I attained that which is supreme; having reached the perfection of direct knowledge, I am now established in the fruit of arahantship.
The faculty of hearing has been purified;
I am one possessed of the threefold knowledge, attained to supernormal powers,
and skilled in discerning the minds of others.
“I ask the Teacher of peerless wisdom,
who cuts through doubts even in this very life:
The bhikkhu has passed away at Aggāḷava.”
"Renowned, illustrious, and with a mind fully extinguished—
'Nigrodhakappa' is the name given by you,
O Blessed One, to that brahmin."
Thus, seeking liberation, he practiced paying homage to him—
energetic and firm in his vision of the Dhamma.
O Sakka, we too, all of us, [pay homage] to that disciple.
We wish to know, O All-Seeing One;
our ears are poised for hearing.
You are our Teacher; you are unsurpassed.
Cut off doubt; speak this to me, O one of vast wisdom, make known him who has attained final Nibbāna;
speak to us in the midst [of our assembly], O you of universal vision.
Like Sakka among the gods, he has a thousand eyes.
Whatever fetters here are paths to delusion,
sides of ignorance, and grounds for doubt;
Having reached the Tathāgata, they no longer exist;
for this is the supreme eye among men.
Indeed, if a person never [yields] to the defilements...
Just as the wind disperses a cloud of mist,
so was the entire world shrouded in darkness that even those possessing light could not shine.
The steadfast become makers of light;
O Hero, I consider each of them to be exactly so.
We have approached the one who possesses insight and knowledge.
Reveal the Dhamma to our assemblies.
Quickly utter your lovely, lovely voice,
cooing softly like a swan spreading its wings.
With well-articulated and melodious voices,
all of you listen with upright minds;
[we shall speak of] him who has abandoned birth and death without remainder.
Having restrained myself, I shall teach the Dhamma to the pure one;
for ordinary people act according to their own desires,
whereas Tathāgatas act with deliberate intention.
This exposition of yours is perfect,
well-grasped by you whose wisdom is upright;
this final salutation with joined palms is offered to you.
Do not delude yourself regarding the wisdom that knows the mind.
Having understood the noble Dhamma in its mutual relationship,
do not delude yourself regarding the energy that knows the mind.
Just as one scorched by the heat longs for water in the summer heat, so do I long for your voice;
rain down the heard teaching!
Whatever purpose I sought when I practiced the holy life—
"Was Kappāyana’s attainment not in vain?
Did he attain Nibbāna, or did he remain with a residue remaining?
We wish to hear how he was liberated."
“He has cut off craving here for name-and-form,” said the Blessed One,
“that stream of darkness which had lain dormant for a long time.”
“He has crossed over birth and death entirely,” so said the Blessed One, the best of the five.
“Having heard this, I have confidence.”
"Your word, O best of seers,
is indeed unfailing; what I have asked has not deceived me, O Brahmin."
As he spoke, so he acted;
such was the disciple of the Buddha.
He cut through the net of Death.
The Blessed One, the one who is appropriate, saw the beginning of grasping— the firm web of the magician.
Truly, you have transcended the aeons,
the realm of death so difficult to cross.
I pay homage to you, the God of Gods.
To you, O supreme among bipeds, I give this son,
born after me, a great hero,
a true-born son of a Naga.”
Thus indeed did the Venerable Elder Vaṅgīsa speak these verses.
The Mahānipāta is finished.
Herein is the summary verse:
In the seventy-ninth chapter,
Vaṅgīsa was the sole possessor of inspired eloquence;
there was no other elder besides him.
The verses are seventy-one.
The Theragāthā is concluded. Herein is the summary verse (uddāna):
There are one thousand verses and three hundred and sixty;
and there are two hundred and sixty elders.
And four [factors] have been proclaimed.
Having let out the lion’s roar,
the sons of the Buddha are free from taints.
Having reached the winter season,
they have been extinguished like a mass of fire.
Thus ends the *Theragāthā-pāḷi*.
